claims.source: For capillaries obstructed with microspheres, almost all recanalized by extruding the obstruction back into the circulation (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, and Figure 2—video 1), while only a small fraction (2%) recanalized by extruding the microsphere through the endothelial wall into the parenchyma, commonly referred to as angiophagy (Figure 2E; Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Figure 2—video 2).
claims.evidence: Figure 2C and supplementary figures show examples of recanalization by extrusion into circulation.

claims.claim: Proximity of the obstruction to the nearest flowing capillary was the only vascular factor that predicted recanalization.
claims.source: The only vascular factor that predicted recanalization was proximity of the obstruction to the nearest flowing capillary (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B).
claims.evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 3B shows significant difference in distance to nearest flowing capillary between recanalized and pruned capillaries.

claims.claim: Capillary branch order, blood flow velocity, or lumen diameter in upstream and downstream capillaries was not predictive of recanalization.
claims.source: By contrast, capillary branch order, blood flow velocity or lumen diameter in upstream and downstream capillaries was not predictive of recanalization (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C–G).
claims.evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 3C-G shows no significant differences in these parameters between recanalized and pruned capillaries.

claims.claim: A subset of capillaries regained blood flow only to be pruned at a later time point.
claims.source: Interestingly by 21 days, 30% of all obstructed capillaries (at time 0) had been eliminated. While one would have expected 20–25% based on recanalization rates in the first 48 hr, we discovered that a subset of capillaries regained blood flow only to be pruned at a later time point (Figure 2F,G, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: Figure 2F,G shows examples and time course of capillaries that recanalized then were pruned.

claims.claim: Delayed pruning could not be predicted by changes in blood flow velocity, width, or flux in the recanalized primary capillary or connected secondary capillaries.
claims.source: This phenomenon could not be predicted by changes in blood flow velocity, width, or flux in the recanalized primary capillary, or connected (secondary) capillaries (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 4 shows no significant differences in hemodynamic parameters for capillaries that were later pruned.

claims.claim: Previously obstructed capillaries that regained flow have a greater probability of experiencing a second obstruction.
claims.source: However, by inducing a second wave of microsphere obstructions (microsphere injections 4 days apart), we noticed that the probability of experiencing an obstruction was greater in capillaries that were previously obstructed and regained flow (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 5 shows significantly higher obstruction probability in previously obstructed capillaries.

claims.claim: Delayed pruning of initially recanalized capillaries could be explained by a second spontaneous obstruction missed between imaging sessions.
claims.source: Therefore, it is possible that delayed pruning of capillaries in ones that initially regained blood flow, could be explained by a second spontaneous obstruction that was missed in the days between imaging (Erdener et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Inference based on finding that previously obstructed capillaries have higher re-obstruction risk and citation to Erdener et al., 2017 on transient obstructions.

claims.claim: There is a 69.8% chance an obstructed capillary will be intact and flowing at 21 days.
claims.source: In summary (Figure 2H), by following capillaries for 21 days after an obstruction, we determined there was a 69.8% chance the capillary would be intact and flowing either by extruding the emboli back into circulation (110/162 capillaries) or through angiophagy (3/162 capillaries).
claims.evidence: Figure 2H summarizes outcomes: 113/162 capillaries (69.8%) were flowing at 21 days.

claims.claim: There is a 30.2% chance an obstructed capillary will be pruned by 21 days.
claims.source: There was a 30.2% chance of being pruned (49/162 capillaries), with no evidence of compensatory sprouting.
claims.evidence: Figure 2H shows 49/162 capillaries (30.2%) were pruned by 21 days.

claims.claim: The likelihood of capillary pruning did not differ significantly between spontaneous and microsphere-induced obstructions.
claims.source: Importantly, the likelihood of capillary pruning did not differ significantly between obstructions that occurred spontaneously versus those that were induced with microspheres (unpaired t-test t(19)=0.72, p=0.48).
claims.evidence: Statistical comparison showing no significant difference in pruning rates between obstruction types.

claims.claim: Capillary pruning led to a transient increase in blood flow velocity in adjacent capillaries, particularly those upstream of the pruned segment.
claims.source: From a hemodynamic perspective, capillary pruning led to a transient increase in blood flow velocity and flux (flux estimates volume of blood flowing per second through a vessel) in adjacent capillaries, particularly those upstream of the pruned segment (Figure 3A–E).
claims.evidence: Figure 3B,C shows increased RBC velocity in upstream capillaries adjacent to pruned segments.

claims.claim: Capillary pruning led to a transient increase in blood flux in adjacent capillaries, particularly those upstream of the pruned segment.
claims.source: From a hemodynamic perspective, capillary pruning led to a transient increase in blood flow velocity and flux (flux estimates volume of blood flowing per second through a vessel) in adjacent capillaries, particularly those upstream of the pruned segment (Figure 3A–E).
claims.evidence: Figure 3E shows increased RBC flux in upstream capillaries adjacent to pruned segments.

claims.claim: RBC velocity, vessel width and flux in control capillaries were stable across imaging timepoints.
claims.source: By contrast, RBC velocity, vessel width and flux in control capillaries such as those from vehicle injected mice (without microspheres), capillaries distant to obstructions or those adjacent to recanalized capillaries were stable across imaging timepoints (Figure 3B–E).
claims.evidence: Figure 3B-E shows stable measurements in control groups (vehicle injected, distant vessels, adjacent to recanalized).

claims.claim: Capillary pruning induces a relatively long-lasting perturbation of blood flow in connected capillary networks over several days.
claims.source: These results show that capillary pruning induces a relatively long-lasting (over several days) perturbation of blood flow in connected capillary networks.
claims.evidence: Conclusion based on hemodynamic measurements showing changes persisting over multiple imaging timepoints.

claims.claim: There is a well-established age-related reduction in capillary density.
claims.source: We first replicated well-established reports of an age-related reduction in capillary density (Brown and Thore, 2011; Riddle et al., 2003; Klein and Michel, 1977; Hinds and McNelly, 1982; Casey and Feldman, 1985; Buchweitz-Milton and Weiss, 1987; Jucker et al., 1990; Amenta et al., 1995a; Jucker and Meier-Ruge, 1989; Amenta et al., 1995b) by comparing vascular networks in young adult and aged Tek-GFP mice (Figure 4A,B; 3–4 vs. 15–18 month-old mice, respectively; 6 and 7 mice per group,>49,000 capillaries).
claims.evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior aging studies and confirmed by current experimental data.

claims.claim: There was a 10 ± 8% loss in capillary density over 13.5 months in aged mice compared to young adult mice.
claims.source: Based on our analysis, we found a 10 ± 8% loss in capillary density over the 13.5 month age difference (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: Figure 4B,C shows quantification of capillary density in young vs aged mice.

claims.claim: Predicted capillary loss (88% remaining) closely matched measured capillary loss (90 ± 8% remaining) in aged mice.
claims.source: Comparing the fraction of vessel loss predicted by our model over the course of ~13.5 months (~405 days, with day 0 representing young adult mouse in Figure 4C), we found close agreement between experimentally observed and predicted capillary loss (predicted = 88% capillaries remaining vs. measured = 90 ± 8%; Unpaired t-test to hypothetical mean 0.88, t(6)=0.68, p=0.52).
claims.evidence: Figure 4D shows predicted vs measured capillary loss with statistical comparison showing no significant difference.

claims.claim: Spontaneous capillary obstruction and subsequent pruning without compensatory sprouting can account for age-related loss in capillary density.
claims.source: Thus, spontaneous capillary obstruction and subsequent pruning without compensatory sprouting, can account for age related loss in capillary density.
claims.evidence: Conclusion based on close match between predicted and measured capillary loss in aging.

claims.claim: VEGF-R2 is a critical regulator of endothelial cell function and is very sensitive to changes in hemodynamic shear stress.
claims.source: We focused on Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor Receptor 2 (VEGF-R2) signaling given that it is a critical regulator of endothelial cell function and is very sensitive to changes in hemodynamic shear stress (Olsson et al., 2006; Tzima et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Olsson et al., 2006 and Tzima et al., 2005.

claims.claim: DiI-coated microspheres leave an indelible stamp of where obstruction occurred, even in recanalized capillaries.
claims.source: As mentioned previously, lipophilic DiI leaches into endothelial cells at the site of the obstruction, therefore leaving an indelible stamp of where the obstruction occurred, even in recanalized capillaries (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: Figure 5A shows DiI labeling in both obstructed and recanalized capillaries.

claims.claim: Obstructed capillaries had significantly lower pVEGF-R2 colocalization compared to sham capillaries 30 minutes after microsphere injection.
claims.source: Consistent with the hypothesis that VEGF-R2 signaling is sensitive to changes in blood flow (27), obstructed capillaries (30 min after microsphere injection) had significantly lower colocalization with pVEGF-R2-labeled capillaries [sham 13.41 ± 2.4% compared to obstructed 3.85 ± 1.3%, unpaired t-test t(30) = 3.86, p=0.0006, n(sham)=3 mice, 16 vessels, n(obstructed)=4 mice, 16 vessels].
claims.evidence: Quantitative immunohistochemistry showing significant reduction in pVEGF-R2 in obstructed capillaries.

claims.claim: Three hours after microsphere injection, recanalized capillaries exhibited two distinct populations based on pVEGF-R2 expression.
claims.source: Three hours after microsphere injection when capillaries have begun to recanalize, we identified two distinct populations of recanalized capillaries based on pVEGF-R2 expression co-localization with DiI-labeled endothelium (Figure 5B, insert).
claims.evidence: Figure 5B shows bimodal distribution of pVEGF-R2 colocalization in recanalized capillaries.

claims.claim: Recanalized capillaries exhibited either significantly lower or higher pVEGF-R2 expression than obstructed or unobstructed control capillaries.
claims.source: Recanalized capillaries exhibited either significantly lower or higher pVEGF-R2 expression, than capillaries that were still obstructed by microspheres or unobstructed control capillaries (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: Figure 5B shows statistical comparison of pVEGF-R2 levels across different capillary states.

claims.claim: VEGF injection (i.c.v.) significantly increased obstruction density 24 hours after microsphere injection compared to vehicle.
claims.source: VEGF treatment significantly increased obstruction density 24 hr after microsphere injection compared to vehicle-injected mice (Figure 5C, unpaired t-test, t(8)=3.282, p=0.01, only cortex contralateral to injection site was analyzed).
claims.evidence: Figure 5C shows increased microsphere density with VEGF treatment.

claims.claim: Tamoxifen treatment in Tek CreERT2 X Kdr+/fl mice significantly reduced vascular pVEGF-R2 expression.
claims.source: Both of these approaches significantly reduced VEGF-R2 signaling as indicated by lower immunohistochemical staining for pVEGF-R2 [Figure 5E; tamoxifen vs vehicle: unpaired t-test, t(6)=3.32, p=0.01; SU5416 vs vehicle: unpaired t-test t(6)=3.17, p=0.02] or western blot detection of VEGF-R2 protein levels in the cortex (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Figure 5E shows reduced pVEGF-R2 immunolabeling with tamoxifen treatment.

claims.claim: SU5416 treatment in Tek-GFP mice significantly reduced vascular pVEGF-R2 expression.
claims.source: Both of these approaches significantly reduced VEGF-R2 signaling as indicated by lower immunohistochemical staining for pVEGF-R2 [Figure 5E; tamoxifen vs vehicle: unpaired t-test, t(6)=3.32, p=0.01; SU5416 vs vehicle: unpaired t-test t(6)=3.17, p=0.02] or western blot detection of VEGF-R2 protein levels in the cortex (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Figure 5E shows reduced pVEGF-R2 immunolabeling with SU5416 treatment.

claims.claim: VEGF-R2 knockdown with tamoxifen significantly enhanced capillary recanalization rates.
claims.source: For both types of analysis, rates of capillary recanalization were significantly enhanced when VEGF-R2 signaling was reduced with VEGF-R2 knockdown (Figure 5F,G) or pharmacological inhibition (Figure 5H, I).
claims.evidence: Figure 5F,G shows increased recanalization and reduced pruning with tamoxifen treatment.

claims.claim: VEGF-R2 inhibition with SU5416 significantly enhanced capillary recanalization rates.
claims.source: For both types of analysis, rates of capillary recanalization were significantly enhanced when VEGF-R2 signaling was reduced with VEGF-R2 knockdown (Figure 5F,G) or pharmacological inhibition (Figure 5H, I).
claims.evidence: Figure 5H,I shows increased recanalization and reduced pruning with SU5416 treatment.

claims.claim: Improved recanalization with VEGF-R2 manipulation was associated with a significant reduction in pruned capillaries at 21 days.
claims.source: Not surprisingly, improved recanalization was associated with a significant reduction in the number of pruned capillaries at 21 days (Figure 5F,H).
claims.evidence: Figure 5F,H shows reduced pruning rates with VEGF-R2 knockdown or inhibition.

claims.claim: VEGF-R2 knockdown or inhibition did not cause global cardiovascular changes.
claims.source: The effects of VEGF-R2 knockdown or inhibition on recanalization rates were not explained by any global cardiovascular changes, as we found no differences in heart rate, breath rate, blood pressure or tissue oxygenation between treated and control groups (Figure 5—figure supplements 1–2).
claims.evidence: Figure 5—figure supplements 1-2 show no significant differences in cardiovascular parameters.

claims.claim: VEGF-R2 manipulation effects could not be explained by differences in initial microsphere density.
claims.source: Further, these effects could not be explained by significant differences in the initial density of microspheres injected [microsphere density 30-min post-injection: vehicle vs. SU5416 = 652 ± 224 versus 562 ± 200 microspheres/mm3, t(6) =0.25, p=0.8; vehicle vs Tamoxifen: 509 ± 234 versus 328 ± 70 microspheres/mm3, t(10)= 2.0, p=0.07].
claims.evidence: Statistical comparison showing no significant difference in initial microsphere density between groups.

claims.claim: VEGF-R2 knockdown or inhibition did not significantly alter RBC velocity in control, recanalized or adjacent vessels.
claims.source: Lastly, VEGF-R2 knockdown or inhibition did not significantly alter RBC velocity in either control, recanalized or adjacent vessels (Figure 5—figure supplements 1–2).
claims.evidence: Figure 5—figure supplements 1-2 show no significant differences in RBC velocity across vessel types.

claims.claim: VEGF-R2 signaling plays a critical role in dictating capillary recanalization.
claims.source: In conclusion, these experiments indicate that VEGF-R2 signaling plays a critical role in dictating capillary recanalization.
claims.evidence: Conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence showing VEGF-R2 manipulation affects recanalization rates.

claims.claim: The mouse cortex occupies approximately 180 mm3.
claims.source: However, it is important to keep in mind that the mouse cortex occupies ~180 mm3 (Badea et al., 2007) with an estimated 3.6 million capillaries (Figure 4) (; Schmid et al., 201719, 33).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Badea et al., 2007.

claims.claim: The mouse cortex contains an estimated 3.6 million capillaries.
claims.source: However, it is important to keep in mind that the mouse cortex occupies ~180 mm3 (Badea et al., 2007) with an estimated 3.6 million capillaries (Figure 4) (; Schmid et al., 201719, 33).
claims.evidence: Calculation based on cortex volume and capillary density, supported by citation to Schmid et al., 2017.

claims.claim: At any given time, one could expect a few hundred obstructed capillaries in the mouse cortex.
claims.source: Therefore, at any given time, one could expect a few hundred obstructed capillaries in the mouse cortex.
claims.evidence: Calculation based on 0.12% obstruction rate and 3.6 million total capillaries.

claims.claim: Over a year, the obstruction and pruning model predicts a 12% reduction in capillary density.
claims.source: For example, our data show that ~30% of obstructed capillaries were eventually pruned with no compensatory sprouting. Over a year, we would predict a 12% reduction in capillary density which closely approximates our experimentally determined estimate of vessel loss, as well as others (; Hinds and McNelly, 1982; ; Buchweitz-Milton and Weiss, 1987; 11-14, 34).
claims.evidence: Prediction based on obstruction rate (0.12% per day) and pruning rate (30%) over one year.

claims.claim: Capillary occlusion alters blood flow in branches up and downstream of the occlusion.
claims.source: This supports previous experimental work (Schaffer et al., 2006) showing that capillary occlusion alters blood flow in branches up and downstream of the occlusion.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Schaffer et al., 2006 and confirmed by current hemodynamic measurements.

claims.claim: Microvessel loss can lead to abnormalities in local perfusion.
claims.source: Other work has shown through modelling that microvessel loss can lead to abnormalities in local perfusion ().
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to modeling study (citation incomplete in manuscript).

claims.claim: Even a small number of pruning events can significantly alter local blood flow and capillary density despite the highly interconnected nature of the capillary bed.
claims.source: Thus, despite the highly interconnected nature of the capillary bed, even a small number of pruning events can significantly alter local blood flow and capillary density.
claims.evidence: Conclusion based on hemodynamic measurements and modeling predictions.

claims.claim: Previous studies have injected relatively large (10-100 µm) microspheres to model multiple small ischemic strokes.
claims.source: Previous studies have injected relatively large (10–100 µm) microspheres in adult rodents to model multiple small ischemic strokes (; ; Rapp et al., 2008; Roos and Ericsson, 1999; ) or to identify novel mechanism of vessel recanalization (Lam et al., 2010; Grutzendler et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior microsphere studies.

claims.claim: Small 4 µm microspheres can be injected through the tail vein instead of more invasive routes required for larger emboli.
claims.source: Due to their small size, microspheres can be injected through the tail vein instead of through more invasive routes, such as the internal carotid artery which is believed to be required for emboli larger than 10 µm to reach the brain.
claims.evidence: Description of methodological advantage based on microsphere size.

claims.claim: The small size of microspheres allows them to be dispersed throughout the brain.
claims.source: The small size of the microspheres allows them to be dispersed throughout the brain.
claims.evidence: Observation from distribution analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: Microsphere injection did not cause detectable changes in global cardiovascular parameters and blood chemistry.
claims.source: First, we have established that our dosage of microsphere injection did not cause detectable changes in global cardiovascular parameters and blood chemistry (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 2 shows no significant changes in multiple cardiovascular and hematological parameters.

claims.claim: Microspheres obstruct vessels in other organs but do not induce cell death or organ dysfunction.
claims.source: Thus, while microspheres do obstruct vessels in other organs, they do not induce cell death, or organ dysfunction.
claims.evidence: Based on Fluorojade C staining and cardiovascular measurements showing no dysfunction.

claims.claim: Rates of capillary recanalization and eventual pruning were similar between microsphere and natural emboli obstructions.
claims.source: Second, how the brain deals with microsphere obstructions yielded similarities with those that occur spontaneously. For example, rates of capillary recanalization and eventual pruning of obstructed capillaries were similar between the two types of obstructions (microsphere vs natural emboli).
claims.evidence: Comparison of recanalization and pruning rates between spontaneous and microsphere obstructions showing no significant difference.

claims.claim: The composition and size of the obstruction likely affects the route of recanalization.
claims.source: Foremost is the fact that the composition (polystyrene microsphere vs. fibrin, blood cells) and size of the obstruction likely affects the route of recanalization.
claims.evidence: Inference based on comparison with prior studies and observation of low angiophagy rates with microspheres.

claims.claim: Low rates of angiophagy with microsphere obstructions likely would not be the case with larger and more natural emboli.
claims.source: While we found low rates of angiophagy with microsphere obstructions, this likely would not be the case with larger and more natural emboli (such as cholesterol or fibrin-based clots).
claims.evidence: Inference based on comparison with Lam et al. study showing different rates with natural emboli.

claims.claim: Lam et al. showed different rates of washout versus angiophagy between natural emboli compared to microspheres.
claims.source: For example, Lam et al. showed different rates of washout versus angiophagy between natural emboli compared to microspheres (Lam et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Lam et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Isoflurane has pleiotropic effects that influence synaptic transmission, blood flow and ischemic cell death.
claims.source: Anesthetics such as isoflurane have pleiotropic effects that influence synaptic transmission, blood flow and ischemic cell death (Santisakultarm et al., 2016; Yamakura and Harris, 2000; Seto et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to studies on isoflurane effects.

claims.claim: A failure to remove obstructions inevitably leads to capillary pruning.
claims.source: Our finding that a failure to remove obstructions inevitably leads to capillary pruning suggests that the accumulation of obstructions over time is at least partially responsible for the loss of microvascular density in aging reported by us and others (Figure 4) (Klein and Michel, 1977; Hinds and McNelly, 1982; ; Buchweitz-Milton and Weiss, 1987; ; Amenta et al., 1995a; Amenta et al., 1995b; Harb et al., 2013) [see (4Riddle et al., 2003) for review, but also (; Hughes and Lantos, 1987) for studies failing to find age related losses in capillaries)].
claims.evidence: Conclusion based on observation that all non-recanalized capillaries were pruned.

claims.claim: The accumulation of obstructions over time is at least partially responsible for the loss of microvascular density in aging.
claims.source: Our finding that a failure to remove obstructions inevitably leads to capillary pruning suggests that the accumulation of obstructions over time is at least partially responsible for the loss of microvascular density in aging reported by us and others (Figure 4) (Klein and Michel, 1977; Hinds and McNelly, 1982; ; Buchweitz-Milton and Weiss, 1987; ; Amenta et al., 1995a; Amenta et al., 1995b; Harb et al., 2013) [see (4Riddle et al., 2003) for review, but also (; Hughes and Lantos, 1987) for studies failing to find age related losses in capillaries)].
claims.evidence: Inference based on modeling showing predicted loss matches measured age-related loss.

claims.claim: Vessel pruning not being compensated for with sprouting should not be viewed as completely surprising.
claims.source: The fact that vessel pruning was not compensated for with sprouting (angiogenesis) is significant, but should not be viewed as completely surprising since other in vivo longitudinal imaging studies of cortical microcirculation have found scant evidence for angiogenesis (at least below the cortical surface) in the mature brain (Reeson et al., 2015; ; Tennant and Brown, 2013; 31, 34, 49, 50).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior longitudinal imaging studies showing limited angiogenesis in mature brain.

claims.claim: Obstructions targeted a small fraction of capillaries and therefore did not lead to hypoxia or cell death.
claims.source: Furthermore, since our obstructions targeted a small fraction of capillaries and therefore did not lead to hypoxia or cell death, the hypoxia-related signals needed to trigger angiogenesis would not be present.
claims.evidence: Based on lack of Fluorojade C staining and low percentage of obstructed capillaries.

claims.claim: Hypoxia-related signals are needed to trigger angiogenesis.
claims.source: Furthermore, since our obstructions targeted a small fraction of capillaries and therefore did not lead to hypoxia or cell death, the hypoxia-related signals needed to trigger angiogenesis would not be present.
claims.evidence: Statement based on established knowledge of angiogenesis mechanisms.

claims.claim: Discrepancies in empirical estimates of capillary loss with age may reflect different methodologies for visualizing capillaries.
claims.source: Discrepancies in empirical estimates of capillary loss with age may reflect different methodologies for visualizing capillaries.
claims.evidence: Discussion of methodological differences between studies using different labeling approaches.

claims.claim: Evans-blue-based estimates of vessel density in young adult mice closely match other published studies.
claims.source: Importantly, our Evans-blue-based estimates of vessel density in young adult mice closely matches other published studies (; Schmid et al., 201720, 33), particularly those by the Kleinfeld lab (; Tsai et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Comparison with published capillary density estimates showing agreement.

claims.claim: Many previous studies in rats used histochemical staining for alkaline phosphatase to estimate vessel density.
claims.source: In contrast, many previous studies in rats have used histochemical staining for alkaline phosphatase (Jucker et al., 1990; Amenta et al., 1995a; ; Amenta et al., 1995b15, 16, 23, 24) or electron microscopy (Casey and Feldman, 1985) to estimate vessel density.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior rat studies using these methods.

claims.claim: Alkaline phosphatase staining assumes ubiquitous vascular expression that does not vary with age.
claims.source: The caveat of using alkaline phosphatase staining is that it assumes ubiquitous vascular expression that does not vary with age (independent of vessel loss), while electron microscopy studies are constrained by very low sample sizes.
claims.evidence: Critical evaluation of methodological limitations in prior studies.

claims.claim: The main mechanism of recanalizing a cerebral microvessel was historically believed to be through Tissue Plasminogen Activator (TPA).
claims.source: Historically, the main mechanism of recanalizing a cerebral microvessel was believed to be through Tissue Plasminogen Activator (TPA), which was provided by microvascular endothelial cells (del Zoppo and Mabuchi, 2003).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to del Zoppo and Mabuchi, 2003.

claims.claim: The window for TPA-mediated recanalization is short in larger vessels.
claims.source: However, previous work has shown in larger vessels the window for TPA-mediated recanalization is short (; Grutzendler et al., 201442, 43), and many types of obstructions are not susceptible to thrombolytics.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Grutzendler et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Many types of obstructions are not susceptible to thrombolytics.
claims.source: However, previous work has shown in larger vessels the window for TPA-mediated recanalization is short (; Grutzendler et al., 201442, 43), and many types of obstructions are not susceptible to thrombolytics.
claims.evidence: Statement based on knowledge of thrombolytic limitations.

claims.claim: Angiophagy was recently discovered in penetrating arterioles and capillaries.
claims.source: The recent discovery of angiophagy (; Grutzendler et al., 201442, 43) in penetrating arterioles and capillaries suggested different strategies exist for clearing obstructions.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Grutzendler et al., 2014.

claims.claim: The finding of an angiophagy-like process replicates previous findings of the Grutzendler lab.
claims.source: Our finding of an angiophagy-like process where endothelial cells engulf and extrude emboli through the vessel wall replicates previous findings of the Grutzendler lab (; Grutzendler et al., 201442, 43).
claims.evidence: Comparison with prior work showing similar observations.

claims.claim: Leukocytes could have engulfed microspheres and transported them across the capillary wall.
claims.source: However, we cannot rule out the possibility that leukocytes (which were not labelled in our study) could have engulfed microspheres and transported them across the capillary wall.
claims.evidence: Acknowledgment of alternative explanation for observed angiophagy-like events.

claims.claim: The manner and frequency of angiophagy-like events is likely influenced by the specific size of emboli and its composition.
claims.source: Further, the manner and frequency of angiophagy-like events is likely influenced by the specific size of emboli and its composition.
claims.evidence: Inference based on comparison with prior studies and observation of low angiophagy rates.

claims.claim: Larger occlusions (>4 µm) would have more severe consequences such as hypoxia and cell death.
claims.source: For example, larger occlusions (>4 µm) would have more severe consequences such as hypoxia and cell death (Hughes and Lantos, 1987) which can trigger major structural changes in the vascular endothelium through hypoxia-inducible factors.
claims.evidence: Inference based on knowledge of ischemia and citation to Hughes and Lantos, 1987.

claims.claim: VEGF-R2 is coupled to nitric oxide and other signaling pathways.
claims.source: For example, VEGF-R2 is coupled to nitric oxide and other signaling pathways (27) that could mediate a change in vessel tone or diameter in the obstructed capillary.
claims.evidence: Statement based on established knowledge of VEGF-R2 signaling (citation 27 in manuscript).

claims.claim: A recent study has questioned the role of NO as a major capillary dilator.
claims.source: However, a recent study has questioned the role of NO as a major capillary dilator (52), thus other pathways may be involved.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation (52 in manuscript).

claims.claim: Hemodynamic forces from up or downstream capillaries are not likely a critical factor in recanalization.
claims.source: We should also note that heamodynamic forces from up or downstream capillaries are not likely a critical factor since measured levels of blood flow or diameter in these capillaries did not precede or predict capillary recanalization (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: Based on analysis showing no predictive relationship between upstream/downstream hemodynamics and recanalization.

claims.claim: Smooth muscle actin-positive pericytes are found at precapillary arterioles and lower branch order capillaries.
claims.source: In particular, smooth muscle actin-positive pericytes, which are found at precapillary arterioles and lower branch order capillaries, have been shown to regulate capillary flow (Hill et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Hill et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Ischemic stroke leads to prolonged pericyte constriction which can limit blood flow in capillaries.
claims.source: Furthermore, ischemic stroke leads to prolonged pericyte constriction which can limit blood flow in capillaries (Hill et al., 2015; Hall et al., 201453, 54).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Hill et al., 2015 and Hall et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Pericytes may contribute to capillary recanalization by regulating microvessel tone or vasomotion.
claims.source: Therefore, it is possible that pericytes may contribute to capillary recanalization by regulating microvessel tone or vasomotion.
claims.evidence: Speculation based on known pericyte functions in regulating capillary flow.

claims.claim: Pericytes are hotspots of matrix metalloprotease activity associated with BBB disruption.
claims.source: Pericytes could also play a significant role in vessel pruning since they are hotspots of matrix metalloprotease activity associated with BBB disruption, (Underly et al., 2017) which is needed for remodeling of the extracellular matrix and basement membrane around capillaries.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Underly et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Distance to the nearest flowing vessel was the only variable that differentiated recanalization success versus failure.
claims.source: The only variable that differentiated recanalization successes versus failure was distance to the nearest flowing vessel, which suggest at least a more complex interplay between vessel tone and heamodynamic forces.
claims.evidence: Based on analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 showing this was the only significant predictor.

claims.claim: The incidence of capillary obstructions and the rate of recanalization and pruning could be strongly influenced by disease states.
claims.source: Although not the focus of the present study, it is very likely that the incidence of capillary obstructions and the rate of recanalization and pruning could be strongly influenced by disease states.

results.result: The authors estimate that approximately 0.12% of mouse cortical capillaries are obstructed each day (lasting >20 min) based on in vivo imaging showing 2 in 20,334 capillaries obstructed over 2 hours and validation with DiI-labeled microspheres showing 3.69 ± 0.97 obstructed capillaries per mm³.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C23, C26, and C27 provide converging evidence from two independent methods (in vivo imaging and DiI microsphere labeling) that yield nearly identical obstruction rates (0.118% vs 0.14% per day). The consistency between methods and the large sample size (>20,000 capillaries) strongly support this quantitative estimate.

results.result: Capillary obstructions occur preferentially in superficial cortical layers and at lower branch orders (peaking at 3rd arteriole branch order), with no significant difference in distribution between spontaneous and microsphere-induced obstructions.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C3, C29-C32 are supported by statistical analyses showing significant differences in branch order distribution (Figure 1C,D with p<0.0001) and depth distribution (Figure 1B). The finding that spontaneous and microsphere obstructions show similar distributions (p=0.65) validates the microsphere model.

results.result: 75-80% of obstructed capillaries recanalize within 24 hours, with no significant difference in recanalization rates between spontaneous and microsphere-induced obstructions.
results.evaluation: Claims C4 and C42 are supported by longitudinal imaging data (Figure 2D) showing recanalization time courses for both obstruction types with statistical analysis confirming no significant difference (p=0.99). The consistency between spontaneous and induced obstructions strengthens the validity of the microsphere model.

results.result: 30% of all obstructed capillaries are pruned by 21 days (49/162 capillaries), with no significant difference in pruning rates between spontaneous and microsphere-induced obstructions.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C53, and C54 are directly supported by longitudinal imaging data summarized in Figure 2H showing 49/162 capillaries (30.2%) were pruned by 21 days. Statistical comparison shows no significant difference between obstruction types (p=0.48), validating the microsphere model for studying pruning.

results.result: Some capillaries that initially recanalized were subsequently pruned at later timepoints, potentially explained by a second spontaneous obstruction occurring between imaging sessions, as previously obstructed capillaries show higher re-obstruction probability.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C48, C50, and C51 are supported by direct observation (Figure 2F,G) and experimental evidence from double microsphere injections (Figure 2—figure supplement 5) showing significantly higher obstruction probability in previously obstructed capillaries. The inference about missed second obstructions (C51) is reasonable given the imaging intervals and higher re-obstruction risk.

results.result: Pruning of obstructed capillaries involves stepwise regression of endothelial cells, with increased endothelial cell nuclei density at pruned branch points suggesting endothelial cells regress and integrate into adjacent capillaries.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C35-C38 are supported by longitudinal imaging showing stepwise pruning progression (Figure 2A) and quantitative analysis showing significantly increased endothelial cell nuclei at pruned branch points (p<0.0001, Figure 2B). The inference about endothelial cell integration (C38) is reasonable based on the increased nuclei density and comparison to developmental processes.

results.result: Capillary pruning is not compensated for by sprouting angiogenesis, with zero sprouts observed in 162 capillaries followed over 21 days.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C40, and C41 are directly supported by the observation of 0 sprouts in 162 capillaries over 21 days from longitudinal imaging. This is a clear negative result with adequate sample size and observation period. The conclusion is appropriately stated as definitive for this experimental context.

results.result: A mathematical model based on measured obstruction rates (0.12% per day) and pruning probability (30%) predicts 12% capillary loss over one year and 88% remaining after 13.5 months, closely matching experimental measurements of 90 ± 8% remaining in aged mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C60, C61, C62, and C81 are supported by the close agreement between predicted (88% remaining) and measured (90 ± 8% remaining) capillary density in aged mice (p=0.52, Figure 4D). The model is based on empirically measured parameters and the prediction falls within the experimental error range, providing strong support for the mechanism.

results.result: VEGF-R2 signaling plays a critical role in dictating capillary recanalization and pruning, as genetic knockdown (tamoxifen in Tek-CreERT2 X Kdr+/fl mice) or pharmacological inhibition (SU5416) significantly enhanced recanalization rates and reduced pruning.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C11, C71-C73, and C77 are supported by converging evidence from two independent approaches (genetic and pharmacological) showing significantly improved recanalization and reduced pruning (Figures 5F-I). The effects are specific as they are not explained by cardiovascular changes, initial microsphere density, or RBC velocity alterations (C74-C76).

results.result: Capillary pruning induces a transient increase in blood flow velocity and flux in adjacent capillaries, particularly upstream of the pruned segment, representing a long-lasting perturbation over several days.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C58 are supported by hemodynamic measurements showing significant increases in RBC velocity and flux in upstream capillaries adjacent to pruned segments (Figure 3B-E), while control capillaries remained stable. The statistical significance and temporal persistence over multiple imaging timepoints support the conclusion of long-lasting perturbation.

results.result: Proximity to the nearest flowing capillary was the only vascular factor that predicted recanalization success, while capillary branch order, blood flow velocity, and lumen diameter in upstream/downstream capillaries were not predictive.
results.evaluation: Claims C46, C47, and C119 are supported by systematic analysis of multiple vascular parameters (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) showing only distance to nearest flowing vessel significantly differentiated recanalized vs pruned capillaries. The comprehensive testing of alternative predictors strengthens the specificity of this finding.

results.result: Obstructed capillaries show significantly reduced pVEGF-R2 expression 30 minutes after obstruction, while recanalized capillaries at 3 hours exhibit bimodal pVEGF-R2 expression with either significantly lower or higher levels than controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C67 are supported by quantitative immunohistochemistry showing significant reduction in pVEGF-R2 in obstructed capillaries (p=0.0006) and bimodal distribution in recanalized capillaries (Figure 5B). The temporal dynamics and bimodal distribution provide mechanistic insight into VEGF-R2's role in recanalization.

results.result: VEGF injection (i.c.v.) significantly increased obstruction density 24 hours after microsphere injection compared to vehicle, suggesting VEGF-R2 activation impairs recanalization.
results.evaluation: Claim C68 is supported by quantitative analysis showing significantly increased microsphere density with VEGF treatment (p=0.01, Figure 5C). This gain-of-function experiment complements the loss-of-function studies (C71-C72) and supports the conclusion that VEGF-R2 signaling negatively regulates recanalization.

results.result: The 4 µm microsphere model successfully obstructs 3.67% of cortical capillaries without causing global cardiovascular dysfunction, cell death, or organ dysfunction, and yields similar recanalization and pruning rates as spontaneous obstructions.
results.evaluation: Claims C33, C86-C90 are supported by comprehensive validation showing no significant changes in cardiovascular parameters, blood chemistry, or cell death markers (Figure 1—figure supplement 2-3), and similar outcomes to spontaneous obstructions. This extensive validation supports the microsphere model as a valid experimental approach.

results.result: Almost all microsphere obstructions (98%) recanalized by extruding the obstruction back into circulation, while only 2% recanalized by angiophagy (extrusion through the vessel wall).
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C45 are supported by direct observation from longitudinal imaging showing 3/162 capillaries (2%) recanalized via angiophagy (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 2). The low rate of angiophagy is acknowledged as potentially influenced by microsphere composition and size (C91-C92).

results.result: On average, there was no significant lasting deformation of newly separated capillaries after pruning compared to controls based on inter-capillary distance measurements.
results.evaluation: Claim C39 is supported by quantitative measurements of inter-capillary distance at time 0 and +21 days showing no significant difference (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). This addresses a potential concern about structural consequences of pruning.

results.result: The rate of capillary obstructions did not differ significantly between awake and isoflurane-anesthetized mice, ruling out spontaneous obstructions as purely artifacts of anesthetics.
results.evaluation: Claim C28 is supported by statistical comparison showing no significant difference in obstruction rates between awake and anesthetized conditions (p=0.29 for volume, p=0.10 for length). This control experiment strengthens the validity of findings obtained under anesthesia.

results.result: VEGF-R2 knockdown (tamoxifen) and inhibition (SU5416) significantly reduced vascular pVEGF-R2 expression without causing global cardiovascular changes, differences in initial microsphere density, or alterations in RBC velocity.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70, C74-C76 are supported by immunohistochemistry and western blot showing reduced VEGF-R2 signaling (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) and comprehensive controls showing no confounding effects (Figure 5—figure supplements 1-2). These controls strengthen the specificity of VEGF-R2 effects on recanalization.

results.result: Delayed pruning of initially recanalized capillaries could not be predicted by changes in blood flow velocity, width, or flux in the recanalized primary capillary or connected secondary capillaries.
results.evaluation: Claim C49 is supported by analysis showing no significant differences in hemodynamic parameters for capillaries that were later pruned (Figure 2—figure supplement 4). This negative result is important for understanding the mechanisms underlying delayed pruning.

results.result: 10 of 16 mice had non-flowing capillary segments present at the start of imaging, indicating spontaneous obstructions were not unique to a few mice.
results.evaluation: Claim C24 is supported by direct observation showing obstructions distributed across 10/16 mice (range 1-4 per mouse). This demonstrates that spontaneous obstructions are a general phenomenon rather than an artifact of individual animals.

results.result: Microsphere obstructions were spread across the cortex affecting all major cerebral vascular territories in an anterior to posterior manner.
results.evaluation: Claim C34 is supported by spatial distribution analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 4) showing microspheres distributed across cortical regions from -2 mm to +1.5 mm relative to bregma. This demonstrates the model produces widespread rather than focal obstructions.

results.result: There is a 69.8% chance an obstructed capillary will be intact and flowing at 21 days, either by extruding the emboli back into circulation (110/162) or through angiophagy (3/162).
results.evaluation: Claim C52 is directly supported by the summary data in Figure 2H showing 113/162 capillaries (69.8%) were flowing at 21 days. This represents a straightforward calculation from the observed outcomes.

results.result: The study replicated well-established reports of age-related reduction in capillary density, with Evans-blue-based estimates in young adult mice closely matching other published studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C59 and C101 are supported by comparison with multiple prior studies (Figure 4A-C) and close agreement with published capillary density estimates, particularly from the Kleinfeld lab. This validation strengthens confidence in the measurement approach.

results.result: The mouse cortex occupies approximately 180 mm³ with an estimated 3.6 million capillaries, suggesting at any given time one could expect a few hundred obstructed capillaries.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C80 are supported by citations to anatomical studies (Badea et al., 2007; Schmid et al., 2017) and straightforward calculation (0.12% of 3.6 million ≈ 4,320 obstructions per day, or a few hundred at any given time). This contextualization helps interpret the biological significance of the obstruction rate.

results.result: The brain is an energetically demanding organ with kilometers of capillaries that are inherently narrow (~3-5 µm diameter) high resistance tubes serving as the primary site of nutrient and gas exchange.
results.evaluation: Claims C12, C13, and C17 are supported by established scientific knowledge and citation to Attwell et al., 2010. These are well-accepted facts that provide important context for understanding capillary obstruction susceptibility.

results.result: Prior literature establishes that cognitive decline with aging and neurodegenerative diseases is associated with capillary loss, capillaries are susceptible to obstruction, and progressive rarefaction of cerebrovascular networks occurs with aging.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C16, C18, and C20 are supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. These claims accurately represent the state of knowledge and provide essential context for the current study's motivation and significance.

results.result: No prior study has comprehensively followed the long-term outcome of capillary obstructions and mechanisms dictating their fate, or tracked obstructions in animal models of vascular cognitive impairment.
results.evaluation: Claims C19 and C126 represent statements about gaps in the literature. While the authors' review of existing studies supports these claims, it is difficult to definitively verify the absence of such studies without exhaustive literature review. The claims appear reasonable based on the cited literature.

results.result: Spontaneous obstructions present with a gap in capillary lumen fluorescence (mean diameter 3.85 ± 1.25 µm) created by stalled cells or debris, and analysis was restricted to obstructions lasting >20 minutes to exclude transient events. DiI-coated 1 µm microspheres can stamp spontaneously obstructed capillaries.
results.evaluation: Claims C21, C22, and C25 describe methodological approaches supported by Figure 1A and citations to prior work on transient obstructions. The DiI microsphere stamping method is a novel technical contribution that is well-described and validated.

results.result: VEGF-R2 is a critical regulator of endothelial cell function that is very sensitive to changes in hemodynamic shear stress, and DiI-coated microspheres leave an indelible stamp of obstruction location even in recanalized capillaries.
results.evaluation: Claim C63 is supported by citations to Olsson et al., 2006 and Tzima et al., 2005, providing rationale for focusing on VEGF-R2. Claim C64 is supported by Figure 5A showing DiI labeling persists in recanalized capillaries. These establish the technical and conceptual foundation for the VEGF-R2 experiments.

results.result: Capillary occlusion alters blood flow in branches up and downstream, microvessel loss can lead to abnormalities in local perfusion, and even small numbers of pruning events can significantly alter local blood flow and capillary density.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C84 are supported by citation to Schaffer et al., 2006 and modeling studies, combined with the current hemodynamic measurements (Figure 3). The integration of prior work with current findings supports the conclusion about the functional significance of pruning events.

results.result: Previous studies used larger microspheres (10-100 µm) to model ischemic strokes, and the composition and size of obstructions likely affects recanalization routes, with different rates of angiophagy expected for natural emboli versus microspheres.
results.evaluation: Claims C85, C91-C93 are supported by citations to prior microsphere studies and Lam et al., 2010. These claims appropriately acknowledge limitations of the microsphere model and contextualize the low angiophagy rate observed.

results.result: Isoflurane has pleiotropic effects that influence synaptic transmission, blood flow, and ischemic cell death.
results.evaluation: Claim C94 is supported by citations to studies on isoflurane effects. This acknowledges a potential confounding factor, though the awake vs. anesthetized comparison (C28) addresses this concern.

results.result: Failure to remove obstructions inevitably leads to capillary pruning, and the accumulation of obstructions over time is at least partially responsible for age-related loss of microvascular density.
results.evaluation: Claims C95 and C96 are supported by the observation that all non-recanalized capillaries were pruned (C35) and the close match between predicted and measured age-related capillary loss (C61). The conclusion is appropriately qualified as 'at least partially responsible' acknowledging other potential mechanisms.

results.result: Lack of compensatory sprouting should not be surprising given prior studies showing limited angiogenesis in mature brain, and the small fraction of obstructed capillaries did not lead to hypoxia or cell death that would trigger angiogenesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C99 are supported by citations to prior longitudinal imaging studies and the lack of Fluorojade C staining (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B). This provides reasonable explanation for the absence of sprouting observed.

results.result: Discrepancies in empirical estimates of capillary loss with age may reflect different methodologies, as many prior rat studies used alkaline phosphatase staining which assumes ubiquitous vascular expression that does not vary with age.
results.evaluation: Claims C100, C102, and C103 provide critical evaluation of methodological differences between studies. The concerns about alkaline phosphatase staining are reasonable and highlight the advantage of the Evans blue approach used in the current study.

results.result: Historically, TPA was believed to be the main recanalization mechanism, but the window for TPA-mediated recanalization is short and many obstructions are not susceptible to thrombolytics. Angiophagy was recently discovered as an alternative clearance mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C108 are supported by appropriate citations to del Zoppo and Mabuchi, 2003 and Grutzendler et al., 2014. These claims accurately represent the evolution of understanding about recanalization mechanisms and contextualize the current findings.

results.result: Leukocytes could potentially have engulfed microspheres and transported them across the capillary wall, and the manner and frequency of angiophagy-like events is likely influenced by emboli size and composition, with larger occlusions having more severe consequences.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C111 represent appropriate acknowledgment of alternative explanations (C109) and limitations (C110-C111) of the microsphere model. These caveats are reasonable and demonstrate scientific rigor in interpretation.

results.result: VEGF-R2 is coupled to nitric oxide and other signaling pathways that could mediate changes in vessel tone, though recent studies question NO's role as a major capillary dilator. Hemodynamic forces from upstream/downstream capillaries are not likely critical factors in recanalization.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C114 discuss potential mechanisms and are supported by appropriate citations and the negative findings in Figure 2—figure supplement 3. These represent reasonable speculation about mechanisms while acknowledging uncertainty.

results.result: Smooth muscle actin-positive pericytes at precapillary arterioles and lower branch order capillaries regulate capillary flow and undergo prolonged constriction after ischemic stroke. Pericytes may contribute to recanalization by regulating vessel tone and to pruning through matrix metalloprotease activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C116 are supported by citations to Hill et al., 2015 and Hall et al., 2014. However, claims C117-C118 represent speculation about pericyte roles in the current context without direct experimental evidence. While reasonable hypotheses, they remain untested in this study.

results.result: The incidence of capillary obstructions and recanalization rates could be influenced by disease states, and this study offers a mechanism for microvessel loss in healthy aging that could extend to risk factors for dementia, providing a framework for understanding microcirculatory changes in cognitive impairment.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C125, C127-C128 represent appropriate discussion of broader implications and future directions. Claims about disease relevance are appropriately qualified as speculation (C120, C125, C127, C128) while being grounded in cited literature about vascular contributions to dementia (C121-C124).
